title: The Shadow Lines
author: Amitav Ghosh
description: Ghosh's narrator remembers a divided subcontinent from a house in south Calcutta, where the streets around Gole Park and the lake hold a family's ordinary life. Memory then jumps the borders the novel calls shadow lines, west to the Prices' London and east to a grandmother's Dhaka, where the 1964 riots turn distance into loss. The map is anchored here in Calcutta, with those two waypoints reaching beyond it.

route.summary: The narrator grows up in a comfortable Calcutta house that his cousins measure themselves against, the fixed point his memory keeps returning to. Ballygunge, a genteel residential quarter of south Calcutta, is the kind of neighbourhood the family belongs to.
route.note: The novel gives the narrator's family a house in south Calcutta but no street address. Ballygunge, the settled middle-class quarter it reads as, is a real district; sited at its centre as the model, not a located building.

route.summary: Gole Park is one of the everyday Calcutta landmarks that fixes the narrator's childhood world to a real map, a busy roundabout at the edge of his family's part of the city. Ghosh uses such named corners to root a story that otherwise ranges across continents.
route.note: Ghosh names Gole Park; this marks the real traffic circle at the Gariahat and Southern Avenue junction that gives the neighbourhood its name.

route.summary: The wooded lake a short walk from the family's quarter is a place of childhood errands and adolescent talk, part of the ordinary Calcutta geography the narrator sets against the far cities of his memory. Long called Dhakuria Lake, it was renamed Rabindra Sarobar for the poet Tagore.
route.note: The lake the narrator walks by is the artificial lake of south Calcutta, known as Dhakuria Lake and renamed Rabindra Sarobar; sited at the lake's centre.

route.summary: In London the narrator's memory settles on the Prices' home on Lymington Road in West Hampstead, the English family whose lives are bound to his own across a generation and a war. The street is real; the house and the family are Ghosh's, a second fixed point to set against Calcutta.
route.note: Outside the Calcutta setting. Ghosh names Lymington Road in West Hampstead, a real street, but the Prices' house is invented; sited on the street as its model rather than a specific number.

route.summary: The grandmother's memory keeps a partitioned family house in old Dhaka, and her return in 1964 draws the narrator's world toward the communal riots and the death that the whole book has been circling. Jindabahar Lane is a real lane in the old city; the divided house on it belongs to Ghosh.
route.note: Outside the Calcutta setting, and across a border. The grandmother's house is placed at 1/31 Jindabahar Lane in old Dhaka, a real lane in the Bangshal and Nazira Bazar quarter; sited there, at the neighbourhood the lane runs through, since the house itself is the novel's.
